text:
卧槽！TradingView 的 K 线形态识别，居然有人做了个加强版！

吞没形态、晨星、锤头线、十字星，不用再一根根找，直接在图表上自动标记，还能设置预警。

这个开源项目叫 all-candlestick-pattern-indicators。

它基于 Pine Script 开发，比 TradingView 自带的形态指标提供了更灵活的筛选和显示设置，源码也全部公开。

核心亮点：

1️⃣ K 线自动识别：支持吞没、晨星、黄昏星、锤头线等经典形态。

2️⃣ 多空信号筛选：自由显示看涨、看跌或中性形态，减少无效信息。

3️⃣ 趋势过滤：支持 SMA50、SMA50 + SMA200，结合趋势判断形态信号。

4️⃣ 自动预警：内置 alertcondition，识别指定形态后可触发 TradingView 提醒。

5️⃣ 自定义图表：调整形态标签、颜色和显示规则，还能查看形态解释。

我觉得它最实用的地方，是把原本靠肉眼寻找的 K 线形态，变成了可以直接研究的量化信号。

比如先通过 SMA 判断趋势，再筛选看涨吞没、晨星等反转形态，结合成交量进一步研究入场条件。

而且可以直接打开源码，研究每种形态的识别规则，再改成自己的 Pine Script 指标。

经常使用 TradingView、研究 K 线形态，或者想开发股票量化策略的，这个项目值得收藏。

https://t.co/LoeTkD0otr

quotedTweet.text:
真有点狠！TradingView 策略调参，居然能直接交给 Python 批量跑了。

从行情下载、策略回测到贝叶斯优化，连最优参数都能自动写回 Pine Script！

项目叫 HyperView，1K Stars、265 Forks，MIT 协议。

它基于 Python、TA-Lib 和 Optuna，把 TradingView 策略研究搬到本地，支持批量回测、参数优化和多品种分析。

以前优化一套交易策略，得反复调整参数、运行回测、比较收益和回撤。现在不少重复工作可以自动完成。

核心亮点：

1️⃣ TradingView 数据：通过 WebSocket 获取历史 K 线，符合条件的账户最多支持约 4 万根。

2️⃣ 本地策略回测：模拟 TradingView 成交逻辑，支持多空交易、止盈止损及组合绩效分析。

3️⃣ 贝叶斯参数优化：利用 Optuna TPE 自动搜索止盈止损组合，比较收益、回撤和 Profit Factor。

4️⃣ Pine Script 优化：支持批量优化部分策略参数，并导出写入最优参数的 Pine 脚本。

5️⃣ 多品种量化研究：支持股票、Crypto 和多时间周期，还能调用 TA-Lib 的 150+ 技术分析函数。

我觉得最实用的，是它把 TradingView 策略研究中最繁琐的调参流程自动化了。

比如研究 MACD + RSI 策略，可以批量测试 AAPL、TSLA 的不同止盈止损组合，再筛选值得进一步验证的参数。

行情下载 → 策略回测 → 参数优化 → Pine 脚本导出。

而且项目文档还提供了 Codex、Claude Code 辅助开发和验证的工作流。

经常用 TradingView、Python 做股票量化，或者想批量优化交易策略的，这个项目值得研究。

https://t.co/pQuwHOcxIN

text:
Most multi-agent work designs the agents.

However, with the current progress in foundation models, the agent is not quite the bottleneck in multi-agent systems anymore, which is why these systems often struggle to beat a single agent.

They scale poorly because every agent inevitably reads more as the group grows, and no change to the agents can fix that.

We propose ScaleMAS, which designs the medium the agents share, and leaves the agents alone. 

We call this medium the substrate, and we see it as a paradigm shift for ongoing and future research on multi-agent systems.

On our substrate, every agent runs the same prompt. No roles, no manager, and no agent ever sends a message to another agent.

Instead, each one searches a shared datastore, reads what it finds, and publishes what it did. It works like Web search over the group’s own work.

And it works better than existing substrates such as a shared context or blackboard, and also better than agent-centric designs such as all-to-all message passing and coordinator-based delegation.

Most importantly, performance keeps rising as agents are added.

On Contradiction Audit, the blackboard-style baseline never exceeds 7% at any group size, while ScaleMAS reaches 50.9% with 128 agents.

It is also cheaper and more token efficient.

On BrowseComp-Plus, 8 ScaleMAS agents reach 60.0% at about the same compute where 16 blackboard agents reach 26.0%.

On SWE-bench Verified, 4 ScaleMAS agents match 8 independent ReAct agents at 80.0% with about half the tokens.

ScaleMAS is extremely robust.

We inject one agent that fails on every step, and the group performs as if nothing had been injected, while the blackboard baseline drops below 1%. 

We also let agents drop out and rejoin at random, and the group keeps working until most of them are gone, while a coordinator-based design falls apart as soon as the coordinator is lost.

LLMs were not trained to be teammates. But given a well-designed substrate, they work together much better and much more efficiently.

Scaling Multi-Agent Intelligence with Substrate-Centric Coordination: https://t.co/03yLb6HwmZ

quotedTweet.text:
Research index (e.g. Google Scholar) is one of the largest collaborative systems where millions of human users build on each other's work across centuries.

How about we build something similar for async LLM agents?

We give agents a minimal hypertextual system. They asynchronously search for and read related work, cite the work that they find useful, and publish (mini-)papers.

Each search returns only the top k papers, ranked by relevance and a PageRank-like citation weight, which bounds the read cost of each agent to O(k), independent of agent count.

We show that performance effectively scales as we keep adding agents, and the system is robust to absence/failures of individual agents.

每次看到有人说内存不就是个周期股、给几倍 PE 都算客气，我就想起 H100 的料单。三千多美元的 BOM，里面最贵的一块不是台积电那颗逻辑 die，是旁边那几摞 HBM，占到一半上下，台积电那部分连它一半都不到。

也就是说英伟达每卖一张卡，付给内存厂的钱比付给代工厂的多。它这两年那么卖力地把三星往第三家供应商的位子上推，就是因为 75% 的毛利率只能从这最大的一行成本里抠。

假设你是英伟达的采购：一年里最大的一笔钱，付给的是一个你换不掉、还在涨价的人。

开发：最近服务器好卡啊，能不能帮我们查查啥问题？

运维：我看看啊，有个叫 business 的进程占了好多 CPU 资源，你们写的什么破代码又来找我？

开发：啊？？我们怎么没印象，你看看这玩意启动命令？

运维：/app/business

开发：你等一下，我问问谁开的

（十分钟后）

开发：问了，没人认识，关了吧

运维：行，kill 了，再看看

开发：不对啊，怎么还卡卡的？

运维：我草，你们这玩意怎么又起来了？

（半小时后）

运维：这次好了，包稳的，这破玩意有点难搞，也不知道到底从哪起来的，我也不敢删

开发：这都能搞定？牛啊，怎么搞的

运维：while true; do ps -ef | grep business | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}' | xargs -r kill -9; sleep 0.1; done

开发：好厉害，虽然没看懂，但是解决了就好

Claude Code 团队公开了他们审代码的做法：代码大约九成由 Claude 写，六月到九月合并的修改翻了一倍多，需要撤回的比例反而降了四成多。

这期用一摞带洞的奶酪片讲这套做法：每道检查都会漏，叠起来就很难漏，底下还有一张网兜底。

片中回答五个问题：哪些修改还要人看，AI 审 AI 会不会没完，审查的 AI 漏了怎么办，人不读代码怎么懂代码，出了事算谁的。人不再逐行读代码，时间花在机器做不好的判断上。

text:
Karpathy just explained how we’ll work with AI next: diagrams and HTML pages instead of walls of text.

Someone already packed it into one skill.

It is called visual-explainer. Your agent turns plans, diffs and recaps into self-contained HTML pages or slide decks that open in the browser.

Repo: /nicobailon/visual-explainer

Install in Claude Code:
/plugin marketplace add nicobailon/visual-explainer
/plugin install visual-explainer@visual-explainer-marketplace

Some commands worth trying first:

1. /diff-review: a visual code review with an architecture comparison

2. /plan-review: checks a plan against your codebase, with evidence for every fix

3. /project-recap: a mental model of the project when you come back after a week

4. /fact-check: verifies a doc against the actual code

And when the agent is about to print a table with 4+ rows, it renders a page instead.

10.5k stars, MIT, works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Pi.

Anthropic engineers already learn their own codebase this way. They ask Claude for a visual explainer of the slice they are about to change.

quotedTweet.text:
Andrej Karpathy just said the hardest part of AI is now reading what it writes.

His advice: ask the model for a diagram instead. Ask for the answer in HTML and you get an interactive page.

ChatGPT just turned that into Intelligent UI. But it works with one model, inside one app. If you build agents, this is how you give yours the same thing, on any model.

Repo: https://t.co/KZ5TuWkdMj

1. Scaffold it: npx @openuidev/cli@latest create --name genui-chat-app

2. Define each piece of your UI with defineComponent and a Zod schema. Hotel card, chart, form, whatever your product already has

3. Call createLibrary, then lib.prompt(). That is your system prompt, and the model can only use what you registered

4. Stream the answer as OpenUI Lang into the renderer. React, Vue, Svelte or Angular, any model, local ones too. 58% fewer tokens than json-render

5. Wire buttons to actions like action:book so the click goes back to your agent as structured values

The order matters more than the tools. Let the agent fetch data first and draw the UI last, that is where the paper got its gain.

text:
对于今天下午的两篇多 agent 系统架构的论文，的确非常有启发，质量都非常的高。其实两篇论文的思路比较像，都是那种通过契约或者竞价这类的契约方式去做到的。而且效果都远远强于目前主流的方式和架构。

要真正把这种契约与市场机制拉进实际的工程系统里，如果我们要把这个机制解构为工程实践，核心其实围绕着三个非常具体的命题展开。
第一个就是这个契约到底怎么做。
很多人第一反应会以为契约是 Agent 之间用自然语言去做，但这在工程上是无法解析的。
在实际代码中，一个不可分拆的原子契约（Atomic Commitment）必须是一个具备强类型约束的状态机对象。

在目前的工程解法中它至少包含这几个：
条件断言，就是输入数据的格式与有效性校验。
交付物，受约方必须返回符合 Pydantic 或 JSON Schema 严格定义的数据结构。

执行该任务允许消耗的最大 Token 数、最大时间配额（Timeout）或网络重试上限。

SLA 与质量承诺，输出结果的置信度门槛，例如核心字段抽取完整度需达到 95% 以上。
一旦超时或校验未通过，触发哪个具体的补救回调。

这种设计的精髓在于只要契约一旦被双方签署，两个 Agent 之间除了传递执行结果之外，完全零通信。这直接斩断了多 Agent 之间无休止的扯皮，把通信开销降到了物理极限。
第二个就是竞价机制是如何天然解决异构调度与成本控制的。

在传统的中心式系统里，调度代码往往充斥着大量脆弱的硬编码规则。这类规则维护成本极高，且无法应对现实多变的情况。

而基于竞价的自编排如 MPT 论文所展现的，其本质是在解决以最低成本找到最合适节点的资源配置问题。

面对一个网页解析任务，黑板广播任务需求。确定性正则脚本 Worker 基于模板匹配度，报出极低的出价，然后呢轻量小模型 Worker 报出中等出价。最后才是昂贵的高阶多模态 Worker 报出极高出价。

清算系统天然会优先把任务判给最廉价、最敏捷的节点。只有当低价节点违约也就是契约断言失败时市场机制才会逐级触发高价节点的再竞价。

这在系统层面自动实现了最优的成本降级阶梯，完全不需要人工去手写复杂的路由树。

第三点就是对系统容错的重塑。

第一篇论文RCM最漂亮的一个洞察是委派出去，并不意味着免除责任。

在过去的主从系统中，Supervisor 把任务拆给 Agent A，A 又派给 B，B 一旦超时或报错，异常往往会一路击穿堆栈，最终在最外层的 Supervisor 处崩溃。

而 RCM 的局部编排机制定义了严格的责任隔离区：
* Agent A 接了上游的任务，A 与上游签了契约
* A 发现需要辅助，决定将某个子步骤外包给 Agent B
* 此时，B 是对 A 负责，而不是对全局中枢负责。A 必须承担 B 失败时的第一清算人角色
* 如果 B 跑偏了，A 在局部发现违约，A 必须在自己的预算配额内就地自愈，尽全力向上游履行初始契约。只有当 A 尝试穷尽局部资源依然失败时，才会作为不可抗力违约向上汇报。

这种策略网络彻底阻断了由于单一底层叶子节点报错而引发的系统性大溃退。

此外对于工程落地时必须要攻克的两个点我认为如下
尽管这一架构在理论和实验中表现惊艳，但如果要把它应用到目前做的内核，有两个关键瓶颈必须在架构设计时避免。
过度竞价带来的协议税，抓取解析是一个高吞吐场景。如果一个页面里的 50 个列表项，每一项都要在 Agent 之间发起一轮完整的广播、出价、清算闭环，竞价本身的通信和模型推理延迟会彻底拖垮系统吞吐。
工程解法：引入长协机制对已知进行常态化，直接跳过竞价，默认复用历史胜出的契约通道。仅在遇到未知结构时，才动态唤醒竞价市场。

然后就是模型的过度自信与恶意虚标问题。LLM 天生对自身的置信度缺乏校准。一个弱模型可能会为了抢单，虚标自己的能力参数或盲目给出高置信度承诺。

工程解法：底层黑板必须为每个 Worker 维护一个客观信誉积分。报价必须结合该 Worker 过去 100 次执行同类任务的真实断言通过率进行加权折算。一旦发生违约，直接扣减信用权重，从系统层面抑制模型的盲目竞价。

text:
把 ChatGPT 的订阅额度接入 DeepSeek Harness，摆脱codex 5小时限制带来的困扰，让长任务继续飞驰！！！

刚跟 ChatGPT 聊了一个需求：

能不能把我的 ChatGPT 订阅接入 DeepSeek Harness 桌面客户端，直接使用订阅额度，不用单独购买 API？

ChatGPT 给了我两个方案：

1、手动安装插件，按照教程一步一步配置、授权、调试。

2、直接交给 Codex，让它帮我完成整个接入过程。

text:
I don’t ask Claude to “make a video” anymore

I give it 6 small jobs. each one produces one file, and the next job starts from that file

> reference  spec.md
it watches a video I like and writes down why it works: pacing, first motion, cut rhythm

> data  data.json
it pulls the real numbers and keeps the source next to every figure

> story  story.md
one point, one hero number, three beats. before anything moves

> motion  Scene.tsx
it writes every frame as code with Remotion and a motion-design skill

> direct  timing.ts
I give notes in plain words. “title is a beat late”  one line changes

ship  final.mp4
it renders stills, checks them against the spec and the data, then waits for my approval

why small jobs work better:

each step has one clear output, so it’s easy to check
if something looks off, you know exactly which file to fix
nothing gets re-rolled, so the rest of the video stays the same

one big prompt gives you a guess
six small jobs give you a video you can actually edit

full setup, prompt and the 10 open-source skills are in the article

再次隆重给大家介绍一位超级投资人---仙道（金明）

回想起7 月底本末社区香港Money Frontier 活动，我全程都在。印象比较深的分享是超级君 @Super4DeFi 讲了跨市场套利实操与低借高贷。3D 老师 @22333D讲了数字资产的演进

而仙道（金明）作为压轴嘉宾登台，讲了视频这段（第二人生实操手册），我整个人被震撼得头皮发麻。金明不仅仅是世界记录保持者，更是一位超级投资人....

很多兄弟让我出总结，但这场我坚决不放任何 AI 总结，强烈建议大家沉下心来，起码完整看上两三遍

感谢 @vctbtc 分享这段视频，之前我一直以为没人录像只存了录音转写，没想到还能看到完整超清现场🫡

quotedTweet.text:
想给大家隆重介绍一位超级投资人--仙道（金明）

在 7 月底本末社区的 Money Frontier 活动上，他作为压轴嘉宾登台，我当时在台下听完他整场分享，整个人被震撼得说不出话，这是我见过最好的公开演讲之一....而在这次Coinbase线下交易赛里，他是唯一一个没有X账号的

这条录音我到现在还收藏着，给了我不小的震撼

【关于仙道（金明）】
他是极链科技创始人（阿里网易投资 10 亿）、湖畔大学四期学员；2016 年 38 美元买入 Coinbase 股票持仓 8 年没卖，特斯拉 8 美元拿了 10 年；同时也是双破世界纪录的自由潜水世界冠军（潜深 311 米，闭气 9 分 08 秒），33 岁检测生理年龄 18 岁

───
他在活动现场分享了自己的实盘数据：

• 2024 年加密资产收益约 380%，2025 年约 8%，2026 年截至 7 月为 +3%（最大回撤 26%）

• 2025~2026 年实物卡牌组合收益约 370%，宝可梦“御三家”三年涨幅超 1000%，持有的 PSA 9 分皮卡丘卡三年涨了 10 倍以上（同款今年拍卖成交超 1.2 亿人民币）

• 2026 美股 YTD 收益约 65%：重仓闪迪、谷歌、SOSL，近期加仓海力士，938 抄底智谱、1300 半仓止盈 4 天赚近 40%，平仓 Palantir 和奈飞

───

【现场分享的投资底层认知】

1. 核心资产与“水晶球问题”：
仙道：美元过去 20 年 M2 年均增速 9%，人民币超 11%，面对巨额债务央行不可能停印，BTC 长期必涨；问明天涨不涨是骗人的“水晶球问题”，回调时左侧加仓拉低买入成本才是对的

2. 实物资产的“无用性法则”：
仙道：引用同学王宁的话“越有用的东西越贬值”，手机数码等功能性物品一定会贬值；反而是顶级宝可梦卡、艺术品这种“无用”、易存储、全球统一定价的文化资产，放 10 年反而涨几十上百倍

3. Body Time 与多做好事：
仙道：“时间不是唯一的资产，有身体的时间才是”。33 岁测出生理年龄 18 岁，靠冷水敷脸降心率皮质醇、全暗恒温睡眠、补肌酸；99% 的成功来自时代运气，利他才能接住好运

───

这次 @coinbase 邀请他出战线下实盘赛，我猜很大一个原因是他本身就是 Coinbase 最早期的股东之一？

并且他在美股、Crypto 、链上套利等各个赛道全都是顶级实力，实在太厉害了，有谁知道在哪里能看到更多的分享吗？

他是极链科技创始人（阿里网易投资 10 亿）、湖畔大学四期学员；2016 年 38 美元买入 Coinbase 股票持仓 8 年没卖，特斯拉 8 美元拿了 10 年；同时也是双破世界纪录的自由潜水世界冠军（潜深 311 米，闭气 9 分 08 秒），33 岁检测生理年龄 18 岁

───
他在活动现场分享了自己的实盘数据：

• 2024 年加密资产收益约 380%，2025 年约 8%，2026 年截至 7 月为 +3%（最大回撤 26%）

• 2025~2026 年实物卡牌组合收益约 370%，宝可梦“御三家”三年涨幅超 1000%，持有的 PSA 9 分皮卡丘卡三年涨了 10 倍以上（同款今年拍卖成交超 1.2 亿人民币）

• 2026 美股 YTD 收益约 65%：重仓闪迪、谷歌、SOSL，近期加仓海力士，938 抄底智谱、1300 半仓止盈 4 天赚近 40%，平仓 Palantir 和奈飞

───

【现场分享的投资底层认知】

1. 核心资产与“水晶球问题”：
仙道：美元过去 20 年 M2 年均增速 9%，人民币超 11%，面对巨额债务央行不可能停印，BTC 长期必涨；问明天涨不涨是骗人的“水晶球问题”，回调时左侧加仓拉低买入成本才是对的

2. 实物资产的“无用性法则”：
仙道：引用同学王宁的话“越有用的东西越贬值”，手机数码等功能性物品一定会贬值；反而是顶级宝可梦卡、艺术品这种“无用”、易存储、全球统一定价的文化资产，放 10 年反而涨几十上百倍

3. Body Time 与多做好事：
仙道：“时间不是唯一的资产，有身体的时间才是”。33 岁测出生理年龄 18 岁，靠冷水敷脸降心率皮质醇、全暗恒温睡眠、补肌酸；99% 的成功来自时代运气，利他才能接住好运

text:
This is f*cking insane.

Chinese researchers just dropped a paper with a title that will make every agent framework nervous: "The End of Harness Engineering".

The argument fits in one line: writing the program around the model is finished as a skill.

A harness written by a human is one person's guess about one task on one afternoon. It ships, nobody re-reads it, nobody scores it, and the agent runs that guess for months.

A harness written by the loop is a file that grades itself. A small 4B model reads what failed, writes 8 edits, and only the edit that scores best on held-out questions survives.

The big model never changes. The file around it does, every round.

So the human job collapses to one artifact: the scoring set. You write the questions, never the program.

Frameworks turn disposable. The exam turns into the job.

That is the exact loop I built and documented below: one https://t.co/JlQQhqH44N, 300 Kimi K3 workers, 37 rewrites in 41 rounds, zero opened by me.

The whole paper in one line: write the exam before the code ↓

text:
Cal AI 今年被 MyFitnessPal 收购了，据报道收购前 12 个月卖了 4000 多万美元。

看了一期 Starter Story Build（视频链接见评论），请的是他们的 CMO，拆解当时怎么请人帮他们做流量。我觉得做 marketing 的话，有很多东西可以学：

1. 不找大网红，而是找普通人，专门为你的 App 开一个新号。先每条 10 美元试 10 条，效果好的再签每月 30 条、每条 30 美元，然后复制铺量。

2. 新号要先养。每天花 30 分钟刷同领域的视频，先发几条不提品牌的内容，等有一条破了 1000 播放再发推广，避免被平台限流。

3. 内容形式要看产品。如果你的 App 有让人很惊喜的瞬间，就做病毒式的故事，追求播放量；如果没有，就先把痛点讲透，再引出 App，追求转化。

4. 最后算账。他举了个例子：花 900 美元买 30 条视频，拿到 60 万播放，每千次播放的成本（CPM）是 1.5 美元；最后带来 120 个付费用户、2400 美元收入，每千次播放的收入（RPM）是 4 美元。RPM 大于 CPM，才值得加大投放。

所以我觉得，花钱请人推广，说到底是一个数学问题，靠数据驱动。先用数据筛选创作者，数据好、内容好的再去铺量，同时一直算投入产出比，这样买量才有效。

你觉得这套花钱买量的方法行得通吗？试过的朋友也欢迎分享一下效果。

text:
Most developers accept the very first code solution an AI gives them.

Boris Cherny (the creator of Claude Code at Anthropic) shared the exact prompts their internal engineering team uses to force better output:

1. The "Elegant Rewrite" Prompt:
When the AI gives you a messy, band-aid fix that technically works, reply with:

"Knowing everything you know now, scrap this and implement the elegant solution."

2. The "Reverse PR Review" Prompt:
Before opening a Pull Request, flip the roles and make the AI test you:

"Grill me on these changes and don't make a PR until I pass your test."

3. The "Behavioral Proof" Prompt:
Instead of asking "Does this work?", say:

"Prove to me this works by diffing the behavior between main and this feature branch."

Stop treating coding agents like autocomplete. 
Push them like a senior engineer reviewing a draft.

关心办公领域Agent开发的小伙伴可以看下这个框架。现在大量Agent宣传自己都是靠几个demo案例，要么就是通用benchmark刷分。但是真正要在工作中可靠地跑起来，需要对真实场景做扎实的评测和迭代。只是如果你自己来亲手做这一切，会非常复杂。有很多地方要自己造轮子。

有了RSI自我改进提升机制以后，改进本身可能AI也能帮你做了，但是搭建这个系统依然是件繁琐的事。

LlamaFactory团队之前就推出了PenguinHarness这样一个开源的harness框架，现在把所有的算法和 Benchmark 都做成插件，同时把RSI自我改进提升的算法整理出来开源，也放出自制的真实办公场景评测集。

不论是自我学习，AI科研，工作应用，还是开源贡献，都值得一看。未来有什么好用的实践案例，大家也可以一起分享。

再说了，巨头们无论造出多好用的agent，不还是要从咱们身上收钱。支持开源就是支持未来的科技平权！

quotedTweet.text:
大家好！很高兴分享我们团队的开源新作 PenguinHarness～

在 Github 获得了 7 万 Star 以后，我们正在打造自进化（RSI）领域的 LlamaFactory，志在成为统一、高效、稳定、灵活的 Agent 自进化框架。

一句话介绍：
🐧 我们开源了 Multi-Agent 自进化框架：PenguinHarness，将所有 RSI 算法集成到一个统一框架中，现已获得了 2600 Github Stars。

📖 为了更全面地了解现有 RSI 工作，我们详细调研了 140 篇论文，将它们归纳整理分类，形成了 awesome-rsi 仓库，并发表了综述 paper。

📊 为了公平对比不同算法的自进化效率，我们构建了自进化 Benchmark：GDPevo。涵盖 6 大企业场景、240 个 Task，对 6 种主流 Agent 进行了评测。

以下为详细介绍：

和 LlamaFactory 的思路一样，我们想把所有和 RSI 有关的数据、模型、算法和评估都集成到一个开源 Harness  框架里面，方便大家实验和调试。现在已经集成了 5 种 RSI 算法和 7 个 Benchmark，未来我们的目标是扩充到 100 多个。同时，我们借鉴 DSH 的 Everything is Plugin 思路，把所有的算法和 Benchmark 都做成插件，相互解耦，让用户可以灵活调用任意 RSI 算法进化不同的 Agent。我们也做了精美的客户端，任何操作系统都可以一键安装，本地运行，可以到官网下载最新版体验。
项目官网：https://t.co/CvMVlaA6Kj
开源仓库：https://t.co/OYXXTp50PL

为了对现有学界工作有更好的理解，我们开源了 awesome-rsi  仓库，并且发表了综述论文，对近期的 140 篇工作进行了梳理，还把 RSI 的发展路线和深度学习的路线进行了对照，发现很多概念都是一一对应的，只不过现在的对象变成了 Agent。
开源仓库：https://t.co/DpjwtGnqcg
论文链接：https://t.co/DMJNFIPUxJ

为了更好地评估不同 Harness 与方法的自进化效果，我们做了 GDPevo Benchmark，涵盖 6 大真实企业场景，共 240 个任务。通过进行 Train-Val 划分，在防止过拟合的前提下公平评估 Agent 的自进化能力。
开源仓库：https://t.co/Eiwlc9ExOD
论文链接：https://t.co/cYINn4R8A0

这条帖子不仅仅是介绍我们的工作，还希望能号召各位学界、工业界的伙伴来参与我们的开源项目。如果你也想在开源项目署名，共同发表论文，欢迎私信详聊～

text:
verifying the science of LLM training is just a function of compute, and as compute scales you can almost infinitely parallelize and compress time

math was even easier, tons of existing data, you only need inference tokens, it's extremely parallelizable and proofs almost never have negative second order interactions with each other

even if model training is less of a perfect testbed than math, there is no doubt this will happen too. the big difference is that it needs 2*compute (inference and A LOT of training compute) so much less accessible, but the dynamics are the same

labs have spent enormous effort figuring out the right metrics for training. for pre-training it's relatively straightforward - which is also good news for tracking RSI - you establish a scaling ladder and measure the "efficiency gain": for a given budget, how much does a new proposal save compared to baseline to reach the same metric?

the question is how you define this "efficiency gain", which efficiency (flops? time? KV cache? data efficiency?..) and which gain (val loss? knowledge? reasoning?..)

i think it's quite similar for post training (modulo reward hacking), i would hope it's similar for alignment as well but after listening to @dwarkesh_sp <> @polynoamial itw i'm not sure as the "gain" here would assume that we have a correct way to measure behavior without eval awareness, probably other stuff i'm not thinking of here

anyway, when you put all of this together, hard to not believe in RSI

quotedTweet.text:
how do you trust your agents' work more? copy this post/link and give it to your @bot or agent!

1. codebase improvements: this is just good software engineering - better architecture, stronger types and invariants, clear boundaries. agents love to copy what exists and take the shortest path, so make the easy thing the right thing. categorically eliminate problems through code and you won't need to think about it again.
2. static analysis: lint rules, tests, CI, verification (eg TLA+). very token efficient ways to catch issues ahead of time.
3. prose: comments, rules, AGENTS.md, skills - anything that can't be enforced and requires agent judgment. use it minimally, but do use /create-verification-skill.
4. human review: the hardest to scale. at the rate agents land code, it's pretty much impossible to thoroughly review every PR, so spend that effort on the highest leverage point, designing an environment where agents do the right thing by default.

this forms an inverse pyramid: you want most of your effort at the top, least at the bottom. codebase improvements are deterministic, making it more token efficient, and lets you sleep more soundly at night.

install https://t.co/u9xIlN3eN0 and create a new Project:
1. look through my slack/chat messages and code review comments where i've given feedback on PRs, code, architecture
2. use /recall on my past transcripts to learn how i steer agents
3. /poteto-mode use /correct and /architect on past commits to find the most common pitfalls agents fall into, then propose a plan to rearchitect the code i own so it's more agent friendly. answer open questions with prototyping rather than defer to me, and back the plan with real data. 
4. before you begin, use /sharpen + /in-your-own-words and confirm this prompt with me

text:
Must-read paper integrating decision models like Jev into harnesses.

They distilled an open 4B decision model, mostly from Jev's answers on the agent's own states, that beats Jev inside that agent and is much cheaper to run.

Their harness, JevAgentHarness, sends each routine choice to the decision model and uses its answer only when the confidence clears a threshold fitted on the agent's own trajectories. Below the threshold, the LLM decides as usual. With the fitted threshold, tool and argument cascades cut cost by 14.2% without changing the outcome of any of 500 tasks. A fixed threshold of 0.5 lost 21.5 points.

They also train AgentDecision-4B on states the agent reaches after its own mistakes, with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% with it and 82.0% with Jev. On familiar tasks, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1 to 89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster while staying within 3 points of success.

Paper: https://t.co/WQ5tyTlh5K

一个人扛自媒体，真正磨人的往往不是写内容，而是那套天天重复的流程：追热点、定选题、写文案、做封面、剪片子、发平台、盯数据。

Easel 这个开源项目，直接把这套活儿交给 AI Agent 去跑。

它由浙大和北大两个实验室做出来，定位是社媒运营 Agent，跑在 OpenClaw 上，把热点发现、内容策划、图文视频制作、多平台发布、数据复盘串成一条完整工作流。

更关键的一点：它会为每个账号积累长期画像，把定位、受众、内容风格、平台限制和历史表现都记下来。发布后的数据还会回流，让下一轮产出越来越贴账号本身。

等于给单打独斗的自媒体号，配了一支会自己复盘的 AI 内容团队。

DeepSeek says V4.1-Flash-1017 was trained for their own harness, so I tested it.

Same model (deepseek-flash API, thinking high), same 34 coding/shell/git tasks, 2 runs each, interleaved.

Quality tied (407/408 passed). But DeepSeek Harness took 1.63x the time and 1.91x the output tokens vs minimal Pi.

Swapping Pi's tool schemas to DSH's: 1.34x slower. Switching Pi to DeepSeek's Messages API: 0.81x, slightly faster.

Harness matters, and more harness isn't better.

text:
💰 In April 2002, $SKHY Korean manufacturer Hynix was drowning in debt. Micron offered about $3.4B in stock for its DRAM memory business. The Hynix board voted unanimously, "no".

A decade later, telecom giant SK acquired Hynix, who experimented with AMD to build the first version of the modern HBM-wired GPU. For years it barely sold. Samsung competed but exited the market in 2019. 

When AI arrived in 2024, @NVDA needed this new type of HBM memory and $SKHY was the perfect partner. Today it makes about 60% of the world's HBM, it's worth more than $1T, and in July it listed on Nasdaq as $SKHY.

Sometimes a "no" is the best thing that can happen to you.

昨天我的eian-riso-broll Skill破 200+ Star 🌟啦。
正式介绍一下它的黄金搭档：⁠eian-collage-broll⁠。  
它用来覆盖另一些B-Roll场景🎬，给观点和金句配 B-roll，所以这个 Skill，专门用来把口播变成「纸拼贴定格风」的视觉隐喻画面。
只需要在 Codex 里上传你的定稿口播文案，其它的交给Skill搞定。
收到文案后，会先提取文案里的视觉隐喻，构思画面画面，在生成首尾帧图片，外带一份视频生成提示词。把素材丢进视频模型，生成竖屏 B-roll 画面。整体的风格是拼贴风格的定格动画。
为了保持视频整体的一致性统一采用暖色纸底/黑白剪贴人物/彩色卡纸/硬投影 + 9 套配色

text:
Anthropic 最新这份报告，已经把 AI 未来的「认知差」直接量化出来了。

91% 的 Anthropic 员工认为，到 2030 年 AI 能做出诺奖级发现，美国公众只有 39%。超过一半 Anthropic 员工预计 AI 能完成自己至少 80% 的工作，普通美国人只有 5%。

而且双方对「自动化越多，失业压力越大」这套逻辑其实差不多。能拉开判断的，是他们每天接触到的 AI 能力完全不同。

Anthropic 内部已经有点像提前进入未来了。Agent 工作时长是员工的 6 倍，初级技术岗位的新招聘占比从 27% 降到 9%，新的瓶颈开始变成人的注意力和判断。

这样看的话，很多关于 AI 的分歧，可能只是大家活在不同的能力版本里。

如果前沿实验室真的是一个领先指标，那今天听起来很激进的工作变化，未来可能会随着 Agent 普及慢慢变得普通。

当然，Anthropic 本身是极端的 AI-native 公司，不能直接外推整个社会，这一点也很重要。

https://t.co/cbUWAnLq8b

都给我去看这些 AI 播客！顺便练练英语！真正的差距，来自你是否在听"第一手的人"说话。这几个YouTube播客，让你直接和这个行业的"源头"对话：

1️⃣ AI & I
这个播客是Every做的，核心探讨AI会如何改变"个体"的工作方式？会讲非常多AI + 个体创业，AI工具如何改变生产力，超级个体的未来形态等。

2️⃣ Lenny's Podcast
产品经理 + 增长 + AI的顶级播客。如果你只选一个播客长期听，我会选这个。Lenny会邀请一线操盘手，直接讲"他们是怎么做增长的"。最近AI相关内容非常多，比如AI产品怎么做PMF，AI公司怎么冷启动。

3️⃣ Peter Yang
最适合"轻量高效吸收"的 AI + 产品内容。他的内容有一个特点：非常结构化 + 非常实用。你能快速学到AI产品设计思路，Prompt / workflow以及如何用AI提升工作效率。

4️⃣ The a16z Podcast (AI 专题/系列)
VC视角看AI的"钱往哪里流"。如果想知道AI的机会在哪里？哪些赛道正在被资本押注？那这个必须听。内容会更偏行业趋势和创业方向，有技术vs商业的判断。

5️⃣ Google DeepMind Podcast
最接近"AI源头"的内容，这个播客的嘉宾基本都是真正在做AI模型的人，内容会更偏模型能力边界和AGI讨论。有点难，但信息密度极高。

6️⃣ Latent Space
AI圈最"内行"的播客之一。这个播客很有意思，它是那种AI从业者听给AI从业者的内容，你会听到很多最新模型讨论，开源vs闭源，还有AI infra / agent的内容，如果你能听懂，说明你已经在圈子里了。

7️⃣ The AI Daily Brief
每天10分钟，跟上AI世界，这是我最推荐"日更补信息"的一个。更新快，信息密度高，不废话。适合碎片时间听，帮助你减少碎片时间的胡思乱想。

text:
notes on using AI productively:

- you can separate most work into two buckets: AI-verifiable and not. how you should work depends on which bucket your work falls into

- "verifiable" boils down to whether AI can independently tell (verify) if work that it completes is good or not.

- if your work is verifiable, design a verifier or system of verifiers and "let 'er rip." use as much AI as you can and get out of the way. you're not the bottleneck anymore, so no marginal attention is required as tasks scale.

- if it might be verifiable, you can try building an AI judge. but you need evals to test the judge's competence. @hammer_mt is my go-to on how to do this well. if you can get your judge good enough, you have verifiable work. back to throwing as much ai at your work as you can

- sometimes a good judge is easy to build, sometimes it's so hard that you may as well not bother.

- if your work can't be verified by an AI, that leaves you or someone else as the judge. treat it like the olden days but with AI help. one or two tasks at a time, avoid context switching, protect your focus

- sometimes, there are verifiable sub-tasks within larger pieces of work. The same process re: judgment and eval-building applies to these sub-tasks. The more you can automate these away, the more you can focus on the pieces that you're uniquely suited for.

@carmenli , CEO of @silicondata and @computeexchange , joins the show to explain how compute is becoming a brand-new asset class. 
A former energy options market maker at DRW who later ran global data integrations at @Bloomberg , Carmen was pre-seeded by DRW founder Don Wilson to build the GPU industry benchmarks. Silicon Data is the referee "the Bloomberg for compute" while Compute Exchange is the liquidity layer where GPUs, tokens and servers change hands.
We get into why token price indexes are falling, recent token & model consumption trends, why GPU residual values are above accounting depreciation schedules, and how neoclouds, their lenders, and compute users can hedge GPU exposure to reduce business volatility.

• "The A100 has been around for six years at this point, and we still see three-year contracts signed on A100s." Residual values are still hovering above five-year straight-line depreciation.

•  “we'd definitely be looking at 30 trillion of [GPU] derivatives every year."

Topics: Compute as an asset class, GPU indices, CME compute futures, GPU depreciation and useful life, neoclouds, token pricing, AI chip supply chain,

💡 This episode is presented by: @OxfordDataPlan –The Home of Alternative Data

*Not Investment Advice.

Highlights:

(0:00) Doug introduces Carmen Li, CEO of Silicon Data and Compute Exchange
(0:20) From energy options market maker at DRW to Bloomberg Data, and why AI startups' swinging GPU costs made compute an industry-wide hedging problem
(4:09) How DRW founder Don Wilson pre-seeded Silicon Data, and building products with no product or sales team
(6:10) Two sides of the coin: Silicon Data as "the Bloomberg for compute" and Compute Exchange as "the Nasdaq for compute"
(7:49) Licensing indices to CME for H100 and B200 compute futures, and four ETFs filed before the futures even trade
(10:22) What makes an index the source of truth: tracking supply-demand, resisting manipulation, staying neutral
(12:57) Normalizing 50 B200 server configurations, and what earns a premium or a discount to the benchmark
(16:04) Sizing the market: from 1–3 trillion in spot compute to a potential 30 trillion in derivatives notional
(18:13) Who hedges first: neoclouds, hyperscalers and the financiers holding GPUs on their balance sheets
(21:06) Michael Burry's depreciation bear case vs. the physical market: A100s still signing three-year contracts after six years
(22:49) Why older chips stay productive: cooling, floor weight, wait times and the second-hand market
(26:20) 300+ neoclouds and why more data sources make an index harder to manipulate
(28:48) B200s at ~$5 per GPU hour, the implied forward curve and the shift into contango
(31:18) Why an index provider can't give forward guidance, or own the assets it measures
(33:59) Token indices on the Bloomberg Terminal, and a leading indicator for AI revenue
(37:03) Why token prices are falling: workflows moving to open-source and open-weight models
(38:51) Token pricing has no transparency, and why customers will demand control
(41:49) Where to invest in the AI stack, lessons from the internet era and why "AI is a gigantic baby"
(45:03) Homegrown silicon, fab capacity and why a hundred chip designers can't create a bubble
(48:56) Why compute futures enable price discovery, not a bubble
(49:29) Running a data company and a marketplace at the same time
(52:47) Carmen's lesson for entrepreneurs: pick something you love
(54:08) The vision: the liquidity provider and the referee for every layer of the cake

quotedTweet.text:
I've spent years in China building robots. I can tell you this playbook won't work:

Pre-seed $: Invent the ultimate actuator.
Seed $$: Figure out mass production.
The hard part isn't inventing a beautiful topology. It's process engineering.

The real delta between the US and China is the ability to execute the enormous amount of physical x mental work required to iterate thousands of times on product designs and manufacturing processes. Partly because much of the tacit knowledge / management systems has left the US, but also because of the sheer human labor required.

This isn't something you can solve by buying traditional automation lines either. It requires:

1. Ideation driven by human intuition. Walking up and down the line, talking to assembly workers, and developing hypotheses about what and where improvements can be made. Raw human hours and attention spent understanding a specific manufacturing process.

2. Large batches of experiments across multiple variables. Coordinating experiments that can easily involve 50+ people, issuing instructions, and tracking the execution and results of each experiment.

3. Purpose-built test design to identify key metrics. For example, a change in gear hobbing profile might require accelerated aging tests on a dyno, while a change in bearing tolerance might require NVH testing.

4. Data + human intuition-driven analysis. Interpreting test results and deciding whether to implement a process change or run the next set of experiments.

5. Strict process control. Reissuing work instructions to the line and ensuring every process is followed to the letter.

The best manufacturers in Asia, from Foxconn to TSMC, have built their competitive advantage on systematically turning thousands of physical experiments into better manufacturing processes.

Their moat isn't just production scale. It's the organizational machinery that makes manufacturing learn and improve faster than anyone else.

I don't think most people in SF clock this.

Say you're manufacturing actuator gears in-house in the US. After you've made your first article, will you hire a team of 10 process engineers to coordinate the 50 technicians running concurrent experiments with designs, processes, and materials?

To understand wear patterns across every pin in a cycloidal drive after 10,000 hours? To reduce backlash from 15 arcmin to 5, then to 1? Just to keep pace with China's progress over the next few years?

Do you have the skill set and management systems in place to do this?

That's why our approach isn't just to automate manufacturing. It's to automate the process of learning how to manufacture better.

Automate simulation and design optimization.

Automate assembly and physical testing.
Automate the design and execution of process experiments.
Feed real-world experimental data back into simulation to continuously improve sim-to-real accuracy.
The goal is to turn what currently takes 50 engineers coordinating thousands of experiments into a closed-loop system that continuously learns and improves.

Then the same robotic line mass-manufactures the product.

PS: Coming back to actuator design, many actuator designs are already commoditized in China. The project in the video is open source, and CNC machining cost in China is just $27 (watch the video).

I hope people understand this reality. I'll link more examples in the replies.

text: I guess AI is moving to the edge much faster than I thought

quotedTweet.text:
Are Small Models Really a Threat?

The Anthropic Fear Factory just released a new report warning that small models may be only months away from self-replicating across cheap IoT devices like off-brand Android TV boxes and smart ovens. They say such an AI worm would be hard to shut down since there’s no central kill switch.

We’ve gone from “The Terminator is coming” to “your toaster might kill you.”

But the experiments don’t support the dramatic headlines. They ran a 26B model across 15 $55 TV boxes at 0.39 tokens per second. The end-to-end test used emulated devices with deliberately open ADB ports, so the “hacking” step was trivial. The capable model often ran on a separate server. Agents were harnessed and told to propagate. This is not proof of autonomous rogue AI worms in the wild.

Nor is the threat even novel. Worms that do this without AI already exist. Mirai in 2016 scanned for default credentials and built massive DDoS botnets. Kimwolf has infected over two million devices, mostly cheap Android TV boxes, by hitting open ADB ports.

Small models don’t currently add much that matters on these targets. The bottleneck has never been figuring out the device. It’s the huge number of devices that ship with open ports, default passwords, and no patching. Traditional worms already exploit that at scale.

A practical attacker would use the best models available offline to design a better traditional worm, then ship the lean binary. You get the intelligence benefit at design time without dragging a slow, heavy model along with every infection. Embedding a weak model in the payload is the worse option for anyone who actually wants the largest, fastest botnet.

The timing of Anthropic’s latest scare campaign is hard to ignore. The day before, Brian Armstrong posted that Coinbase fine-tuned an open-weight small model (Qwen-3.5-9B) on proprietary fraud data. It beat frontier models, including Anthropic’s own Opus 4.5, while being faster and much cheaper. In testing it cut fraudulent transactions by about 30%.

This is the emerging pattern. For narrow enterprise workloads you don’t need a general superintelligence. You need a small specialist model trained on your own data. Cheaper to run, especially as compute gets tighter, and often better on the metric that matters. That is a direct threat to the frontier-company model of selling access to ever-larger general models.

Safety advocates should be welcoming this development. If the real concern is existential risk from ever-larger frontier systems — the ones that could theoretically do sustained autonomous R&D or become hard to control — then a shift toward smaller specialized models is the safer outcome. 

Small models specialized on fraud detection or support tickets are not pushing the frontier. They are not in the category of systems that could become a new species. The theoretical loss-of-control risk is created by models getting bigger and more generally capable.

Safety advocates focused on those risks should welcome companies having a cheaper alternative to constantly scaling general models. Instead we get dramatic warnings about small models at the exact moment they are starting to take real enterprise share from closed-model companies like Anthropic.

text:
In recent days, we have seen reports of developers using AI to recreate software like Photoshop and other Adobe applications as free, open-source alternatives.

We believe that LLMs are now extremely capable at reverse engineering and decompilation. This makes it increasingly important for software developers to protect their code, either by implementing protection themselves or by investing in a software protector such as Dhaedalida or a similar product.

We conducted a small test on an application we created. On the unprotected version, AI generated a working keygen in 3 minutes. After we protected it with Dhaedalida, the model stopped after more than 4 hours without producing a working keygen.

A simpler algorithm still fell, even with protection. Licensing design and protection both matter.

Read the full experiment in the first reply.

I've seen people talking about Solomon being a total mystery but he's actually got the craziest lore if you know occult stuff. The occult myth of King Solomon was that he bound 72 demons to his will using his ring, which was engraved with his seal, and we see him wearing a ring on each figure bearing Chess pieces. The demons were the "Pawns" that he used to construct Jerusalem, but what's also interesting is that demons were also known as Jinn, which Mirage is tied to.

Another interesting thing is that his chessboard looks like an ornate book, with the Ars Goetia being a grimoire of sorcery based on the Testament of Solomon. He's also recreating the occult hand signs of "As above, so below" in this render, with his lower hand forming the Below sign with the chess piece, and the upper hand representing the Above.

So could Solomon be some guy that discovered the actual Ars Goetia and gained magical power through it and is now calling himself Solomon as a point of hubris? Or is this the actual King Solomon whose mystical command over demons has shifted to command over chess pieces? Who knows, but Solomon isn't some unknown mystery, the Deadlock devs know what they are doing.

text:
“Crown Jewel”

Talk about love, clear and true.
Explore and learn, discoveries anew.
To think you have what time can’t touch,
A heart with love ample enough.

Control, illusions conceal,
A world meant to reveal.
In love, there’s pain just as real.
Now you know life’s meant to heal.

Questions, doubts, fear’s ugly snout,
Seen, heard, your senses burn out.
You survive the hell, fire, and rage;
Submit to no one, love with no cage.

Your time will come; death will fall,
Your journey defined once and for all.
Looking back to see a crown jewel,
Unseen to those, all the love in you.

-RJS

Refined by @ChatGPT 

We speak of love beneath a boundless sky,
And search for truths no reason can supply.
We think we’ve found what time can never claim,
A quiet light that burns beyond its flame.

We build our walls to keep the storms outside,
Yet fear becomes the place where shadows hide.
Then love arrives and breaks the walls of stone,
Revealing wounds we never knew we’d known.

Through sleepless nights, the mind begins to race,
While doubt and sorrow wear a thousand faces.
Yet through the fire, we learn to stand alone,
With hearts unchained, belonging to our own.

The years will fall like leaves upon the ground,
Until the final silence comes around.
And when the world releases all we’ve made,
What mattered most will never truly fade.

For hidden deep beneath the scars we bear,
Are countless moments filled with love and care.
And when we leave this world we’ve traveled through,
The crown was always all the love in you.

由 Kabir Oberai 等 13 位贡献者打造的 xtool，目前已在 GitHub 斩获 11.8k Stars——它正试图用纯开源的方式，把 iOS 开发从 Xcode 的围墙花园里解放出来。👇

We need to put more energy into

Which model should think?

text:
In 1525, at Pavia, the finest knights in France rode against lines of Spanish arquebusiers. The knights had trained since childhood.

Many of the gunmen had been handed their weapons a season or two earlier. It didn’t matter.

The French cavalry was shot to pieces and their king was taken prisoner.

Here is how one of those knights might have remembered it:

The Lament of a Knight of the Old Blade

(found, it is said, in a soldier’s prayer book after the battle of Pavia, 1525)

I learned the sword when I was small,
my father’s hand upon my own;
he taught me how to feint and fall,
to read a man by breath and bone.

Twelve winters in the fencing yard,
twelve summers bleeding in the sun,
until my wrist grew quick and hard
and I could best near anyone.

They spoke of it in Milan first,
a thing of iron, fire and smoke,
a hollow staff with thunder cursed
that slew a knight before he spoke.

We laughed. What honour has a tube?
What art lies in a powder flask?
A ploughboy or a village boob
could learn it ere he drained his cask.

At Pavia the morning came
all grey with mist along the wall;
we rode in silk and sang the name
of every saint to guard us all.

I saw them kneel in muddy rows,
those lads who’d never held a blade,
and heard a crack like breaking boughs,
and watched the flower of France unmade.

Old captains fell whose names were sung
in every hall from Rhône to Seine;
the ball that found them had no tongue
to ask their lineage or their pain.

I spurred. I swear I reached a man,
a boy, his beard not yet begun;
he fumbled with his powder pan,
and I could see he longed to run.

And there it was, the thing I’d kept
for forty years: the perfect stroke.
I raised it, and the morning wept,
and somewhere to my left, the smoke.

O Isabeau, I wrote you songs
of how a knight should die for love,
of honour righting ancient wrongs
beneath a watching God above.

But do not sing of how I lie
here in the ditch among the reeds;
there is no ballad for a sky
that rains down lead on noble deeds.

Hang up my blade above the hearth
and polish it on holy days,
but teach our son another worth,
for steel has had its age of praise.

The world has found a quicker art
that needs no breath, no eye, no years.
It does not choose a single heart.
It only multiplies the tears.

I keep hearing his voice in today’s conversations about AI.

“What art lies in a prompt?”

“Anyone could do it.”

“It has no soul, no craft, no years behind it.”

All true, in a sense. The knight’s skill was real. Forty years of discipline is not nothing, and the boy with the powder pan had none of it. The knight’s mistake was not valuing his craft. It was assuming the battlefield would keep valuing it the same way.

And here is the uncomfortable part. Someone who feels this way about AI could write a poem very much like this one. Beautiful, mournful, full of honour and loss. But that is about as far as the attitude can take them. A lament is the last thing a refusal produces. It is a fine thing to hang above the hearth. It is not a strategy.

The nobles who did well after Pavia were not the ones who kept arguing with the gun. They became the officers, the tacticians, the people who decided where the guns would point. The skill that survived was judgment, not the sword arm.

That is the question worth asking now: which part of what you do is the sword arm, and which part is the judgment?

P.S. The poem above was written by an AI, on request, in seconds. Make of that what you will.

Really enjoyed You Can See Everything. Might be most meta documentary ever.  

No spoilers but will say this interview Christopher Nolan did with Nathan Fielder about his show “The Curse” — explaining his creative process — really comes through in Holmes film:

▫️setting the tone is his top priority, even moreso than narrative (“when you have the tone right, everything falls into place”) 

▫️Fielder says he “stumbles into ideas he gets excited about” without a master plan and “just piles things on and it grows” (for the Holmes doc, he had an agreement with A24 to scrap the project even after years of shooting if he didn’t think there was a film)

▫️the musical score is crucial in setting the tone (the sound doesn’t even have to match action on the scene, it can float above just setting mood)

▫️he doesn’t want to rush scenes; let them develop to the point where audience is expecting any action to be consequential and it builds the tension (inspired by old detective TV show Columbo)

***

Full interview here (Nolan really is a Fielder Stan): https://t.co/j1RUbAxTaU

The Louisiana Army National Guard is proud to recognize Brady Guillot, a senior at West Monroe High School, and Ra’Ziya Baity, a senior at Ouachita Parish High School, as recipients of the Future Leader Award, presented as part of the K104 Scoreboard Show!

Brady was presented his award by Sergeant First Class Jamie Trujillo, while Ra’Ziya was recognized by Staff Sergeant Bryson Gipson.

In the Army, leadership is defined as the activity of influencing people by providing purpose, direction, and motivation to accomplish the mission and improve the organization.

The Future Leader Award recognizes high school seniors who demonstrate those same qualities through their character, initiative, leadership potential, and positive influence on others. Brady and Ra’Ziya are already making a difference in their schools and communities, and we’re proud to recognize them as Future Leaders.

👏 Congratulations, Brady and Ra’Ziya! Continue to lead, influence others, and leave every organization better than you found it.

We would also like to thank All Star Trophies for teaming up with the Louisiana Army National Guard to help make the Future Leader Award possible and recognize outstanding young leaders throughout our area.

Could you be one of our next Future Leaders?

The Louisiana Army National Guard develops leaders and provides opportunities to serve, earn money for college, develop career skills, and make a difference in your community and across Louisiana.

text:
CritPt and Humanity's Last Exam were a big step for AI evals. They got working physicists to write genuinely hard, research-level problems and gave the field something real to measure against.

A new paper from researchers at Yale, Jump Trading, Cambridge and USC builds on that work. They had experts re-grade six physics benchmarks and found that many of the questions models were getting "wrong" were actually ambiguous or misgraded. 

Anthropic's latest system card found something similar with its own expert-corrected version of CritPt.

The part that stuck with me is the discussion. The authors say the field now needs "a new style of benchmark for frontier models, built from new hard physics tasks and adequately verified," that it "will likely require substantial financial resources," and that one path is "open competitions in the style recently adopted in mathematics."

That's pretty much what we've been building with AIPhO, the AI Physics Olympiad. It's modeled on AIMO: new, unpublished problems from paid expert writers, every problem reviewed and blind-testsolved by 2–3 people, open-weight models only, and a $250K+ prize pool on Kaggle. Winners release their methods.

The competition runs April–June 2027. If you write physics problems, train open models, or want to get involved, reach out at https://t.co/84oZbRT6b4
